Triggers.value: A memory of the event coming to mind suddenly

Maladaptive Strategies.value: rehearse what to say before any interaction

Threat.value: Having strong negative feelings such as fear, horror, anger, guilt, or shame
I feel unsafe unless my back is against a wall where I can see the room
My body reacts to danger before I have even had time to think

Memory.value: Sometimes I can recall what happened but feel completely numb, as if it happened to a stranger
When I try to explain what happened I lose the thread and cannot finish
When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event.

vignette: Eight years ago, Tavita, an American of Pacific Islander descent, found his firm dispatching him to a regional trade symposium in the Middle East. What began as a standard site inspection quickly unraveled when local tensions erupted into lockdowns. He was moved repeatedly by armed men, hands bound, held in windowless storage containers and locked service corridors. The guards spoke rapidly in Arabic, their voices sharp and unrelenting. Every metallic click of a heavy door, every sudden shift in footsteps, became a marker of absolute helplessness. When he finally returned to his California home, the world had not faded back to normal; it had simply learned a new set of rules. His days settled into a rigid geometry of avoidance and hyperawareness. He found himself angling his drafting table so his back pressed firmly against the studio's load-bearing brick. If he didn't, the air felt thin, unsafe. His heart would hammer, his palms would go slick, his breath would shorten before his conscious mind could even name the threat. The body moved first, always first. At the same time, his studio, once a place of open floor plans and glass partitions, felt like a collection of the confined spaces he had survived. He began declining site visits, claiming scheduling conflicts, and let detailed paperwork pile up on a side table. He avoided work, while at the same time, the central islands and large windows of his studio left him exposed. He told himself he was simply waiting for the right conditions to return, though the conditions never aligned with his expectations. In the quiet hours, when he was alone in the house his late wife had left behind, the past did not arrive as a narrative. Sometimes it came as a sudden, intrusive flash that left him staring at the ceiling. Other times, he could recall the details with a flat, emotionless numbness, as if reading about another man's captivity. When he tried to speak of it to his sister, his thoughts would fracture mid-sentence, leaving him watching his own hands while he lost the thread entirely. During these moments, the auditory texture of that place would surface in his mind: the sharp crackle of voices in Arabic, a wordless shouting that carried no need for translation to feel heavy. What frightened him most was not the loudness, but the quiet collapse that followed-sudden surges of fear, horror, and a heavy, unfamiliar shame that pooled in his chest whenever he realized how emotionally vulnerable he had become. He didn't know how to name it without breaking down. Instead, he turned the volume down on his life. He still refuses to sit with his back to an open doorway. He still maps every client floor plan for a secondary exit before walking through the threshold. He rehearses phone calls to suppliers three or four times, shaping the exact tone, the precise pauses, as if a misstep might open a door he couldn't close. When a contractor once called from a cramped home office, Tavita's breath caught instantly. He pictured the walls closing in, the guards pacing just beyond the door, and he ended the call before the man finished speaking. He kept his own studio door open, yet still felt the need to angle his chair toward the brick, scanning the perimeter with the same mechanical routine that had kept him alive in captivity. The studio's large-format printers hummed in the corner, unused, while his own work gathered digital dust on a server he rarely accessed. He didn't know how to bridge the gap between the man who once designed expansive, light-filled spaces and the man who now measured every room in terms of escape routes. At sixty-seven, the silence of his widowed home has grown heavier than the noise he once fled. He came to therapy because he can no longer carry the weight of waiting for conditions that never arrive. He is hoping, if only partially, to find a way to sit in a room without checking the walls, to let a memory arrive without his heart hammering against his ribs, and perhaps, just perhaps, to speak of what happened without his voice dissolving into the middle of a sentence.
